messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Karim

Karim was fifty-five when he was attacked outside his grain storage facility on a humid August evening three years ago. He had stayed late to repair a broken conveyor belt, the kind of task he had done a thousand times across four decades of farming his family's land in central California. Two men emerged from the darkness near the loading dock. He never saw their faces clearly—later, when police asked him to describe them, he could only offer fragments: a tattoo on one wrist, the sound of rapid breathing, the smell of stale sweat and cologne mixing in the warm air. They wanted money. When Karim refused, they beat him methodically, one holding him while the other struck his ribs and face. He remembered falling, remembered the taste of blood, remembered the sensation of being utterly powerless. Then nothing clear until he was on the ground and they were gone, and his own breathing was loud in his ears.

The assault lasted perhaps three minutes. In the three years since, Karim has been unable to assemble those minutes into a coherent story. When his wife Elena asks him what happened, he starts to explain—he was working late, the men came from the west side of the building—but the sequence fragments in his mind, details scatter, and he loses his place mid-sentence. The memory feels borrowed, as if he is recounting something that happened to someone else, something he witnessed rather than lived. He can summon isolated pieces: the smell of sweat, the pressure of hands on his arms, the specific angle of moonlight on the concrete. But they do not connect. There is no thread. This fragmentation has become its own source of distress; he feels as though he cannot fully own what happened to him, cannot integrate it into his life story.

For the first year after the assault, Karim threw himself into work with an intensity that alarmed Elena. He would rise before dawn and work until dusk, then come inside and spend his evenings reviewing crop reports, planning the next season's irrigation schedules, anything to keep his mind occupied and moving. It was during those months that he first noticed the pattern: whenever his own heart raced—whether from exertion in the fields or from the anxiety that had begun to creep into his baseline—the memories would surface in those same fragmented, disorienting pieces. His racing heart became a trigger, a somatic reminder that sent him spiraling into the scattered recollection of the attack. When that happened, he could not sit still. He would immediately find another task, another project, another reason to work. The overworking was not laziness or dedication; it was a form of flight. He had come to believe that if he kept moving, kept his mind occupied, the memories would not coalesce into something he would have to fully feel or understand.

Karim also began to notice people acting suspiciously—a neighbor lingering too long at the property line, a truck that seemed to circle the farm roads more than once. His body would tense, his vigilance would sharpen, and within moments the fragmented memories would intrude again, pulling him back to that August night. When that happened, rumination would take hold. He would replay the assault in disconnected flashes and find himself consumed with thoughts of revenge, imagining scenarios in which he confronted the men, in which he was stronger, faster, in control. These fantasies of retaliation were both a response to his helplessness and a way of keeping his mind engaged—another form of the same driven, relentless mental activity that characterized his days. He had come to believe that if he could just figure out how to get even, how to reclaim some sense of agency, the fragmented pieces might finally make sense.

He also began to dread the anniversary of the assault. August became a month he tried to skip entirely, throwing himself into harvest preparation weeks early or finding reasons to travel. The dates themselves felt dangerous, as if the proximity to that evening might somehow trigger another attack.

Three months ago, Elena confronted him. She said he was disappearing into work, that she barely recognized him anymore, that he needed help. Karim is here now because his wife insisted, because he is exhausted, and because some part of him recognizes that the fragmented memories are not becoming clearer with time—they are becoming more entrenched, more alien, more impossible to integrate. He is afraid that if he stops working, stops moving, stops planning revenge, the memories will finally cohere into something unbearable. He is also afraid that they never will.
